title: Order Statistics, Conditioning, and CLT
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter answers three related questions from one lecture. Given a batch of independent observations, what can be said about their *sorted* values — the order statistics? Given two random quantities, how does learning one change what should be believed about the other — conditioning? And why does the average of many independent observations settle into a normal distribution no matter what distribution the observations themselves came from — the central limit theorem? It assumes comfort with joint densities, the change-of-variables (Jacobian) formula for transformed densities, and the standard named distributions (Uniform, Exponential, Gamma, Beta, Poisson, Binomial, Geometric, Normal). ## Order statistics Start simple: two random variables $X,Y$ with joint density $f_{X,Y}$, and set $U=\min(X,Y)$, $V=\max(X,Y)$. What is the joint density of $(U,V)$? Because $U\le V$ always, $f_{U,V}(u,v)=0$ once $u\ge v$. For $u This is a multinomial probability with three outcomes of probabilities $F(u)$, $f(u)\delta$ (approximately), and $1-F(u)$, so $$ \mathbb{P}\{u\le X_{(i)}\le u+\delta\} \approx \frac{n!}{(i-1)!\,1!\,(n-i)!}\,F(u)^{i-1}\big(f(u)\delta\big)\big(1-F(u)\big)^{n-i}, $$ and dividing by $\delta$ gives the density. **Differentiating the cdf.** $X_{(i)}\le x$ exactly when at least $i$ of the $X_j$ are $\le x$, an event whose probability is a Binomial tail: $$ F_{X_{(i)}}(x) = \sum_{r=i}^n \binom{n}{r} F(x)^r\big(1-F(x)\big)^{n-r}. $$ Differentiating term by term, the sum telescopes — consecutive terms cancel except at $r=i$ — leaving the same density again. ### Special cases worth knowing *Uniform order statistics.* If $X_1,\dots,X_n$ are i.i.d. $\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$, then $f(u)=1$, $F(u)=u$, and $$ f_{X_{(i)}}(u) = \frac{n!}{(n-i)!(i-1)!}\, u^{i-1}(1-u)^{n-i}, \qquad 0x\} = \prod_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}\{X_i>x\} = e^{-(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n)x}, $$ so $X_{(1)}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n)$: the rates simply add. The same survival-function trick handles the discrete analogue — $X_i\sim\mathrm{Geo}(p_i)$ independently — where $\mathbb{P}\{X_{(1)}>m\}=\prod_i(1-p_i)^m$ shows $X_{(1)}\sim\mathrm{Geo}(P)$ with $P = 1-\prod_i(1-p_i)$. The moral of the last two examples: once the variables are not identically distributed, or not continuous, go back to the cdf or survival function directly, rather than reaching for the order statistic density formula, which needs a single common $f,F$ shared by all the variables. ## Covariance, correlation, and the best linear predictor Before conditioning proper, one more piece of machinery: how well can $Y$ be predicted by a *linear* function of $X$? This turns out to be exactly what correlation measures, and it is the linear special case of a question this chapter answers in full generality once conditional expectation is available, later on. The covariance of $X,Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]$, a bilinear operator, $$ \mathrm{Cov}\Big(\sum_i a_iX_i,\ \sum_j b_jY_j\Big) = \sum_i\sum_j a_ib_j\,\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,Y_j), $$ directly from linearity of expectation. Taking $X=Y$ recovers variance as a special case, and bilinearity gives the usual variance-of-a-sum formula, $\mathrm{Var}(\sum_i a_iX_i) = \sum_i a_i^2\mathrm{Var}(X_i) + \sum_{i\ne j}a_ia_j\,\mathrm{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The correlation is the normalized covariance, $\rho_{X,Y} := \mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)/[\mathrm{SD}(X)\mathrm{SD}(Y)]$. Writing it as $\mathbb{E}(\tilde X\tilde Y)$ for the standardized variables $\tilde X=(X-\mu_X)/\mathrm{SD}(X)$, $\tilde Y=(Y-\mu_Y)/\mathrm{SD}(Y)$, and using the elementary bound $ab\le(a^2+b^2)/2$ (and its mirror image $ab\ge -(a^2+b^2)/2$) gives $-1\le\rho_{X,Y}\le1$. The same bound, applied more generally to $Z_1=X-\mu_X$, $Z_2=Y-\mu_Y$ after standardizing, is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\mathbb{E}(Z_1Z_2)|\le\sqrt{\mathbb{E}Z_1^2}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}Z_2^2}$, from which $|\rho_{X,Y}|\le1$ also follows directly. Independent random variables are always uncorrelated, but not conversely — the lecture leaves it as an exercise to produce a pair of uncorrelated random variables that are not independent. What *does* characterize independence is a stronger statement: $X$ and $Y$ are independent if and only if $g(X)$ and $h(Y)$ are uncorrelated for *every* pair of functions $g,h$ — correlation of the raw variables only sees the linear part of a relationship. That last remark is the key to interpreting $\rho_{X,Y}$. Approximate $Y$ by a linear function $\beta_0+\beta_1X$ and measure the error by $L(\beta_0,\beta_1) := \mathbb{E}(Y-\beta_0-\beta_1X)^2$. Minimizing over $\beta_0,\beta_1$ gives $$ \min_{\beta_0,\beta_1} L(\beta_0,\beta_1) = \mathrm{Var}(Y)\big(1-\rho_{X,Y}^2\big). $$ So $\rho_{X,Y}^2$ is exactly the fraction of $Y$'s variance that the best linear function of $X$ removes: $\rho=\pm1$ means $Y$ is exactly linear in $X$; $\rho=0$ means a linear function of $X$ does no better than the constant $\mathbb{E}(Y)$. This is linear regression, arrived at from first principles rather than assumed. ## Conditioning: the discrete case The rest of the chapter is about conditioning — "very important for statistics classes," in the lecturer's words, because statistics is largely the business of updating beliefs about an unknown parameter after seeing data, and that updating *is* conditioning, done correctly. Recall the definition for events, $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A) := \mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(A)$ when $\mathbb{P}(A)>0$. Summing over a partition $A_1,A_2,\dots$ of the sample space gives the **law of total probability**, $$ \mathbb{P}(B) = \sum_i \mathbb{P}(B\mid A_i)\,\mathbb{P}(A_i), $$ and rearranging the two-piece case ($A,A^c$) gives **Bayes' rule**, $$ \mathbb{P}(A\mid B) = \frac{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)}{\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)\mathbb{P}(A)+\mathbb{P}(B\mid A^c)\mathbb{P}(A^c)}. $$ For two discrete random variables $X,\Theta$, defining $\mathbb{P}\{X=x\mid\Theta=\theta\} := \mathbb{P}\{X=x,\Theta=\theta\}/\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\}$ (whenever $\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\}>0$) gives, for each fixed $\theta$, a genuine distribution in $x$. The law of total probability and Bayes' rule for random variables become $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=x\} = \sum_\theta \mathbb{P}\{X=x\mid\Theta=\theta\}\,\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\}, \qquad \mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\mid X=x\} = \frac{\mathbb{P}\{X=x\mid\Theta=\theta\}\,\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\}}{\mathbb{P}\{X=x\}}. $$ **A Poisson conditioned on its own sum.** If $X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda_1)$ and $Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda_2)$ independently, what is the distribution of $X$ given $X+Y=n$? Since $X+Y\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)$ (independent Poissons add), $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=i\mid X+Y=n\} = \frac{\mathbb{P}\{X=i\}\mathbb{P}\{Y=n-i\}}{\mathbb{P}\{X+Y=n\}} = \binom{n}{i}\Big(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\Big)^i\Big(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1+\lambda_2}\Big)^{n-i}, $$ a $\mathrm{Bin}\big(n,\ \lambda_1/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2)\big)$ distribution: knowing the total splits the count between the two sources exactly in proportion to their rates. **Poissonization of the Binomial.** Run the dependence the other way: let $N\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$, and given $N=n$, let $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ — a coin with heads-probability $p$, tossed a *random*, Poisson-distributed number of times, $X$ counting the heads. The law of total probability gives the marginal distribution of $X$: $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=i\} = \sum_{n\ge i}\binom{n}{i}p^i(1-p)^{n-i}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda}(\lambda p)^i}{i!}\sum_{n\ge i}\frac{(\lambda(1-p))^{n-i}}{(n-i)!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda p}(\lambda p)^i}{i!}, $$ i.e. $X\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda p)$. Bayes' rule then gives the posterior for $N$: conditional on $X=i$, $N-i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda(1-p))$. Pushing further, the *joint* distribution of $X$ and $N-X$ (heads and tails) factors, $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=i, N-X=j\} = e^{-\lambda}\frac{(\lambda p)^i}{i!}\cdot\frac{(\lambda(1-p))^j}{j!}, $$ into a term in $i$ alone times a term in $j$ alone, so $X$ and $N-X$ are **independent**, distributed $\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda p)$ and $\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda(1-p))$ respectively. This is worth pausing on: if a coin is tossed a *fixed* number of times, heads and tails counts obviously cannot be independent — they must sum to that fixed number. Making the number of tosses itself Poisson, randomizing away exactly that constraint, is what buys the independence. ## Conditional densities: the continuous case $\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=\theta\}=0$ for a continuous $\Theta$, so $\mathbb{P}(B\mid A)=\mathbb{P}(A\cap B)/\mathbb{P}(A)$ cannot directly define $X\mid\Theta=\theta$. The fix is a limiting argument: conditioning on $\Theta=\theta$ should be the limit, as $\epsilon\to0$, of conditioning on $\theta\le\Theta\le\theta+\epsilon$. Working through the algebra, $$ \mathbb{P}\{x\le X\le x+\delta\mid\theta\le\Theta\le\theta+\epsilon\} = \frac{\mathbb{P}\{x\le X\le x+\delta,\ \theta\le\Theta\le\theta+\epsilon\}}{\mathbb{P}\{\theta\le\Theta\le\theta+\epsilon\}} \approx \frac{f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta)\delta\epsilon}{f_\Theta(\theta)\epsilon} = \frac{f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta)}{f_\Theta(\theta)}\delta, $$ motivating the **definition** $$ f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x) := \frac{f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta)}{f_\Theta(\theta)}, \qquad f_\Theta(\theta)>0. $$ Two structural facts make this usable. First, as a function of $x$ with $\theta$ fixed, $f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}$ really is a density — nonnegative, integrating to $1$, because $\int f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta)\,dx = f_\Theta(\theta)$ by definition of the marginal. Second, and more useful in practice, since the denominator $f_\Theta(\theta)$ does not depend on $x$, $$ f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x) \propto f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta) \quad \text{(as a function of $x$, for fixed $\theta$)}, $$ and the missing normalizing constant is *whatever makes the right side integrate to 1* — it never needs to be found separately if the right side is recognizable as a named density up to constants. This proportionality trick is used everywhere below. **Example: a Gamma split by its own sum.** Let $X\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$ and $\Theta\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\beta,\lambda)$ be independent. What is $X\mid X+\Theta=1$? Working directly from the definition needs the joint density of $(X,X+\Theta)$ via the Jacobian formula, $f_{X,X+\Theta}(x,1) = f_{X,\Theta}(x,1-x) = f_X(x)f_\Theta(1-x)$, together with the fact that $X+\Theta\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha+\beta,\lambda)$; assembling these gives $X\mid(X+\Theta=1)\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$. The proportionality trick reaches the same place with far less bookkeeping: $$ f_{X\mid X+\Theta=1}(x) \propto f_X(x)f_\Theta(1-x) \propto x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1},\quad 01$ the density of $V$ at $v$ is zero and the conditional density is simply not defined there. **Example: a sum and a ratio, conditioned on one factor.** For independent $X\sim f_X$, $\Theta\sim f_\Theta$: conditioning $X+\Theta$ on $\Theta=\theta$ just shifts $X$ by a constant, and conditioning $X/\Theta$ on $\Theta=\theta$ just rescales $X$ by a constant — but both derivations below are worth seeing, since each is used again later. Direct computation, via the Jacobian formula for $u=x+\theta$ (Jacobian $1$) and $u=x/\theta$ (Jacobian $|\theta|$): $$ f_{X+\Theta\mid\Theta=\theta}(u) = \frac{f_{X,\Theta}(u-\theta,\theta)}{f_\Theta(\theta)} = f_X(u-\theta), \qquad f_{X/\Theta\mid\Theta=\theta}(u) = \frac{f_{X,\Theta}(u\theta,\theta)|\theta|}{f_\Theta(\theta)} = |\theta|\,f_X(u\theta). $$ A distributional shortcut reaches the same answer with no Jacobian at all: conditional on $\Theta=\theta$, the variable $\Theta$ simply *is* the constant $\theta$, so $$ (X+\Theta)\mid\Theta=\theta \stackrel{d}{=} (X+\theta)\mid\Theta=\theta \stackrel{d}{=} X+\theta, $$ where the last step drops the conditioning because $X$ is independent of $\Theta$ — and $X+\theta$ has density $f_X(u-\theta)$, matching the direct computation. The same argument gives $f_{X/\Theta\mid\Theta=\theta}(u)=|\theta|f_X(u\theta)$. ### Independence, restated in terms of conditional densities $X$ and $\Theta$ are independent exactly when $f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}=f_X$ for every $\theta$ — equivalently, exactly when the conditional density of $X$ does not depend on which $\theta$ is conditioned on. This is a useful diagnostic, and also a shortcut, as the "distributional" derivations above already show: whenever a conditional distribution can be argued not to depend on the value conditioned on, that argument *is* an independence claim in disguise, and it licenses dropping the conditioning bar outright. **Example: the Gamma/Beta split, again.** $X/(X+\Theta)$ is independent of $X+\Theta$ (a standard fact about the Gamma family), so $$ X\mid(X+\Theta=1) \stackrel{d}{=} \frac{X}{1}\Big|(X+\Theta=1) \stackrel{d}{=} \frac{X}{X+\Theta}\Big|(X+\Theta=1) \stackrel{d}{=} \frac{X}{X+\Theta} \sim \mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta), $$ recovering the earlier answer, this time by dropping the conditioning in the last step because the quantity being conditioned is independent of the event conditioned on. ### The law of total probability and Bayes' rule for densities Rearranging the definition of conditional density gives $f_{X,\Theta}(x,\theta) = f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x)\,f_\Theta(\theta)$, and integrating out $\theta$ recovers the marginal of $X$ — the continuous **law of total probability**: $$ f_X(x) = \int f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x)\,f_\Theta(\theta)\,d\theta. $$ This is a repackaging, not a new fact: applying it with $f_{X+\Theta\mid\Theta=\theta}(u) = f_X(u-\theta)$ from above *rederives* the convolution formula for a sum of independent variables, $f_{X+\Theta}(u) = \int f_X(u-\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)\,d\theta$, and the analogous computation rederives the density of a ratio of independent variables. Convolution, in other words, is a special case of the law of total probability, not a separate technique. Bayes' rule for densities follows by dividing the joint density by the marginal in the other direction: $$ f_{\Theta\mid X=x}(\theta) = \frac{f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x)f_\Theta(\theta)}{\int f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x)f_\Theta(\theta)\,d\theta} \ \propto\ f_{X\mid\Theta=\theta}(x)\,f_\Theta(\theta) \quad(\text{as a function of }\theta). $$ **Example: a Normal mixed over an Exponential variance gives the Laplace density.** Let $\Theta\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1/2)$ and $X\mid\Theta=\theta\sim N(0,\theta)$ — a Normal whose *variance* is itself random and exponential. The law of total probability gives $$ f_X(x) = \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\theta}}\exp\Big(-\frac{x^2}{2\theta}\Big)\cdot\frac12 e^{-\theta/2}\,d\theta. $$ Substituting $\theta=u^2$ turns this into $f_X(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\displaystyle\int_0^\infty \exp\big(-\tfrac{x^2}{2u^2}-\tfrac{u^2}{2}\big)\,du$. At $x=0$ this evaluates directly to $1/2$. For $x\ne0$, differentiating under the integral sign and then substituting $v=|x|/u$ in the result makes the two exponents trade places, and the integral reproduces itself up to a sign, giving the clean differential equation $$ \frac{d}{dx}\log f_X(x) = -\frac{x}{|x|}. $$ Together with $f_X(0)=1/2$ this pins down $$ f_X(x) = \frac12 e^{-|x|} \qquad \text{for all } x, $$ the Laplace (double-exponential) density. A Normal mixed over an Exponential variance produces a heavier-tailed, sharply-peaked-at-zero density: mixing a light-tailed family over an unknown scale parameter is a standard way heavy tails get manufactured. **Example: Normal prior, Normal data.** Let $\Theta\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$ and $X\mid\Theta=\theta\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$. Multiplying the two densities and completing the square in $\theta$ splits the exponent into a piece depending on $\theta$ and a piece that does not: $$ \frac{(\theta-\mu)^2}{\tau^2} + \frac{(x-\theta)^2}{\sigma^2} = \Big(\frac1{\tau^2}+\frac1{\sigma^2}\Big)\Big(\theta - \frac{x/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\Big)^2 + \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\tau^2+\sigma^2}. $$ Integrating out $\theta$ leaves only the $\theta$-free piece, giving the marginal $$ X \sim N(\mu,\ \tau^2+\sigma^2). $$ Dividing the joint density by this marginal instead (Bayes' rule) reads the *other* piece off the same computation: $$ \Theta\mid X=x \ \sim\ N\!\left(\frac{x/\sigma^2+\mu/\tau^2}{1/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2},\ \frac{1}{1/\sigma^2+1/\tau^2}\right). $$ This example is worth naming carefully, because the names recur for the rest of the chapter: the marginal law of $\Theta$ is the **prior**, the law of $X\mid\Theta=\theta$ is the **data model**, and the law of $\Theta\mid X=x$ is the **posterior**. Writing $1/v^2$ for the **precision** of a Normal with variance $v^2$, the calculation says: *posterior precision is the sum of prior precision and data precision*, and the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data. **Example: Gamma prior, Exponential data.** Let $\Theta\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$ and $X\mid\Theta=\theta\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\theta)$. By proportionality, $$ f_{\Theta\mid X=x}(\theta) \propto \theta e^{-\theta x}\cdot\theta^{\alpha-1}e^{-\lambda\theta} = \theta^{\alpha}e^{-(\lambda+x)\theta}, $$ so $\Theta\mid X=x \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha+1,\lambda+x)$ — the Gamma family reproduces itself under Exponential data, exactly as the Normal family reproduced itself above, and the posterior mean $(\alpha+1)/(\lambda+x)$ is again an interpolation between the prior mean $\alpha/\lambda$ and a data-driven quantity $1/x$. ## Mixing discrete and continuous $X$ and $\Theta$ need not be of the same type. There are four cases — both discrete; both continuous; $X$ discrete with $\Theta$ continuous; $X$ continuous with $\Theta$ discrete — and in every case the law of total probability and Bayes' rule keep the same shape: whichever variable is being "summed out" is replaced by an integral if it is continuous and a sum if it is discrete, everywhere else keeping the natural notation ($\mathbb{P}\{\cdot\}$ for discrete, $f$ for continuous). For $X$ discrete and $\Theta$ continuous, for instance, $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=x\} = \int \mathbb{P}\{X=x\mid\Theta=\theta\}\,f_\Theta(\theta)\,d\theta, \qquad f_{\Theta\mid X=x}(\theta) = \frac{\mathbb{P}\{X=x\mid\Theta=\theta\}\,f_\Theta(\theta)}{\mathbb{P}\{X=x\}}. $$ **Example: Beta–Binomial.** Let $\Theta\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$ and, given $\Theta=\theta$, let $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,\theta)$. The marginal of $X$ is $$ \mathbb{P}\{X=x\} = \int_0^1 \binom{n}{x}\theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x}\,d\theta = \binom{n}{x}B(x+1,n-x+1) = \frac{1}{n+1}, $$ using $B(x+1,n-x+1)=x!(n-x)!/(n+1)!$ — so $X$ is **discrete uniform** on $\{0,\dots,n\}$, a fact not at all obvious without doing the integral. Bayes' rule then gives $$ f_{\Theta\mid X=x}(\theta) \propto \theta^x(1-\theta)^{n-x} \implies \Theta\mid X=x \sim \mathrm{Beta}(x+1,n-x+1), $$ with posterior mean $(x+1)/(n+2)$. Writing this as $\frac{n}{n+2}\cdot\frac{x}{n} + \frac{2}{n+2}\cdot\frac12$ shows the posterior mean interpolating between the prior mean ($1/2$) and the maximum-likelihood estimate $x/n$, with the data's weight $n/(n+2)\to1$ as $n\to\infty$ — the same interpolation pattern as the Normal–Normal and Gamma–Exponential examples above, now for a discrete data model. **Example: statistical classification.** Let $\Theta\in\{0,1\}$ with $\mathbb{P}\{\Theta=1\}=p$, and let $X\mid\Theta=0\sim f_0$, $X\mid\Theta=1\sim f_1$ (continuous). The law of total probability says the marginal density of $X$ is a **mixture**, $$ f_X = (1-p)f_0 + pf_1, $$ and Bayes' rule gives the posterior class probabilities $$ \mathbb{P}\{\Theta=1\mid X=x\} = \frac{pf_1(x)}{(1-p)f_0(x)+pf_1(x)}. $$ This is the entire probabilistic content of a two-class classification problem: a mixture model for the data, and Bayes' rule to recover the class posterior from it. Deciding which class to *predict* given $X=x$ is a risk-minimization question, and it is answered properly later in the chapter, once conditional expectation is available. ## Conditional joint distributions and the chain rule Everything above conditions one variable on one other. In general, given $X_1,\dots,X_m,Y_1,\dots,Y_k$, the conditional *joint* density of $Y_1,\dots,Y_k$ given $X_1=x_1,\dots,X_m=x_m$ is defined the same way, as a ratio of joint densities: $$ f_{Y_1,\dots,Y_k\mid X_1=x_1,\dots,X_m=x_m}(y_1,\dots,y_k) := \frac{f_{X_1,\dots,X_m,Y_1,\dots,Y_k}(x_1,\dots,x_m,y_1,\dots,y_k)}{f_{X_1,\dots,X_m}(x_1,\dots,x_m)}. $$ (For discrete variables, replace densities by point probabilities. The multinomial distribution, conditioned on one of its counts $N_1=n_1$, gives back a multinomial on the remaining categories with renormalized probabilities $p_j/(1-p_1)$ — the discrete analogue.) Two consequences of the definition are used repeatedly. First, applying it one variable at a time and multiplying gives a **chain rule** for any joint density, $$ f_{Y_1,\dots,Y_n}(y_1,\dots,y_n) = f_{Y_1}(y_1)\, f_{Y_2\mid Y_1=y_1}(y_2)\cdots f_{Y_n\mid Y_1=y_1,\dots,Y_{n-1}=y_{n-1}}(y_n), $$ and the same factorization holds conditionally on some further $X_1=x_1,\dots,X_m=x_m$ throughout. Second, there is a **law of total conditional probability**: for any further variable $\Theta$, $$ f_{Y_1,\dots,Y_k\mid X=x}(y_1,\dots,y_k) = \int f_{Y_1,\dots,Y_k\mid \Theta=\theta,\, X=x}(y_1,\dots,y_k)\, f_{\Theta\mid X=x}(\theta)\,d\theta, $$ i.e. the ordinary law of total probability, run entirely inside a fixed conditioning event. **Example: order statistics conditioned on the maximum.** Let $U_1,\dots,U_n$ be i.i.d. $\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$. What is the conditional joint density of $U_{(1)},\dots,U_{(n-1)}$ given $U_{(n)}=u$? Dividing the joint order-statistic density $n!$ (on $0 \mathbb{P}\{Y=0\mid X=x\} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases} $$ the **Bayes classifier** — predict the more probable class given the data, using exactly the posterior class probabilities computed in the classification example above. Weighting the two error types unevenly, $R(g) := W_0\,\mathbb{P}\{Y\ne g(X),Y=0\} + W_1\,\mathbb{P}\{Y\ne g(X),Y=1\}$, shifts the decision boundary to $g^*(x)=1$ iff $W_1\,\mathbb{P}\{Y=1\mid X=x\} > W_0\,\mathbb{P}\{Y=0\mid X=x\}$ — the same argument, with the comparison rescaled by relative costs. All four problems are the same problem: for a loss $L(Y,g(X))$, the risk-minimizing $g^*$ is $$ g^*(x) = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{c\in\mathbb{R}} \ \mathbb{E}\big(L(Y,c)\mid X=x\big), $$ found pointwise by fixing $X=x$ and solving a one-variable minimization problem — the law of iterated expectation is what licenses treating $x$ as a constant once conditioned on it, and what turns that pointwise answer back into a function of $X$. ## Conditional variance Analogously, $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X=x) := \mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x))^2\mid X=x] = \mathbb{E}(Y^2\mid X=x) - \big(\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X=x)\big)^2$, and applying this function of $x$ to the random variable $X$ gives $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)$, a random variable, with $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X) = \mathbb{E}(Y^2\mid X) - \big(\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X)\big)^2$. The **law of total variance** decomposes the unconditional variance into a within-condition piece and a between-condition piece: $$ \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\big(\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)\big) + \mathrm{Var}\big(\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X)\big). $$ Expanding both terms on the right and using the law of iterated expectation on $\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(Y^2\mid X))=\mathbb{E}(Y^2)$ collapses everything to $\mathbb{E}(Y^2)-(\mathbb{E} Y)^2=\mathrm{Var}(Y)$, confirming the identity. In words: total variance is the average *within-condition* variance, plus the variance of the conditional means themselves *across* conditions — noise that remains even once $x$ is known, plus variability that would remain even if $Y$ were replaced by its own conditional mean at every $x$. **Example.** For $\Theta\sim N(\mu,\tau^2)$, $X\mid\Theta=\theta\sim N(\theta,\sigma^2)$, the two laws give $\mathbb{E}(X)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ *without* recomputing the marginal density of $X$ from scratch: $$ \mathbb{E}(X) = \mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}(X\mid\Theta)) = \mathbb{E}(\Theta) = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}(\mathrm{Var}(X\mid\Theta)) + \mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}(X\mid\Theta)) = \mathbb{E}(\sigma^2) + \mathrm{Var}(\Theta) = \sigma^2+\tau^2, $$ matching the marginal $N(\mu,\sigma^2+\tau^2)$ derived earlier the long way. **Example: variance of a random-length sum.** Continuing the random-sum example ($S=X_1+\cdots+X_N$, i.i.d. $X_i$ with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, $N$ independent of the $X_i$): conditional on $N=n$, $S$ is a sum of $n$ i.i.d. terms, so $\mathrm{Var}(S\mid N)=N\sigma^2$ and $\mathbb{E}(S\mid N)=N\mu$; the law of total variance gives $$ \mathrm{Var}(S) = \mathbb{E}(\mathrm{Var}(S\mid N)) + \mathrm{Var}(\mathbb{E}(S\mid N)) = \sigma^2\,\mathbb{E}(N) + \mu^2\,\mathrm{Var}(N). $$ Note both terms: even if $N$ were non-random ($\mathrm{Var}(N)=0$), the sum would still have variance $\sigma^2\mathbb{E}(N)$; randomness in $N$ contributes an *additional* term $\mu^2\mathrm{Var}(N)$, purely from not knowing how many terms are being added. ## The central limit theorem The last topic is a different kind of question — not "what is the exact distribution of some function of the data," but "what does that distribution look like *approximately*, for large $n$, regardless of what distribution the data actually came from." **Central limit theorem.** *If $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are i.i.d. with $\mathbb{E}(X_i)=\mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\sigma^2<\infty$, then* $$ \frac{\sqrt n\,(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma} \ \longrightarrow\ N(0,1) \quad\text{in distribution, as } n\to\infty, $$ *where $\bar X_n = (X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n$.* Informally — and this informal restatement is how the theorem gets used in practice — for large but finite $n$: $$ \bar X_n \approx N\Big(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\Big), \qquad S_n := X_1+\cdots+X_n \ \approx\ N(n\mu,\ n\sigma^2), $$ consistent with the exact facts $\mathbb{E}(\bar X_n)=\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n$, $\mathbb{E}(S_n)=n\mu$, $\mathrm{Var}(S_n)=n\sigma^2$, which hold for *every* $n$, exactly, regardless of the distribution the $X_i$ came from. The central limit theorem is the further claim that, in the limit, the entire *shape* of the distribution becomes Normal too, not merely its mean and variance. The remarkable feature is that nothing about the distribution of the $X_i$ enters the conclusion beyond its mean and variance: the theorem is **distribution-free**. That this is not vacuous is worth checking case by case, against exact facts already available about specific sums: - **Bernoulli.** $X_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)$: $\mathbb{E}X_i=p$, $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=p(1-p)$, and $S_n\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ *exactly*, so the CLT says $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is approximately $N\big(np,\,np(1-p)\big)$ for $n$ large and $p$ fixed. (This special case — the CLT applied to Bernoulli data — was proved by de Moivre in 1733, well before Laplace's general CLT of 1810.) - **Poisson.** $X_i\sim\mathrm{Poi}(\lambda)$: $\mathbb{E}X_i=\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\lambda$, and $S_n\sim\mathrm{Poi}(n\lambda)$ exactly, so the CLT says $\mathrm{Poi}(n\lambda)$ is approximately $N(n\lambda,n\lambda)$ for $n$ large and $\lambda$ fixed. - **Gamma.** $X_i\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha,\lambda)$: $\mathbb{E}X_i=\alpha/\lambda$, $\mathrm{Var}(X_i)=\alpha/\lambda^2$, and $S_n\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(n\alpha,\lambda)$ exactly, so the CLT says $\mathrm{Gamma}(n\alpha,\lambda)$ is approximately $N(n\alpha/\lambda,\,n\alpha/\lambda^2)$ for $n$ large. - **Chi-squared.** A $\chi^2$ variable with $1$ degree of freedom is $Z^2$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$, which is exactly $\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2,1/2)$; a sum of $n$ i.i.d. copies is exactly $\mathrm{Gamma}(n/2,1/2)$, to which the same Gamma reasoning applies. In every one of these cases an exact, named distribution for $S_n$ was available anyway; the point of listing them is that the *same* Normal approximation, built from nothing but the mean and variance, applies whether or not such an exact distribution exists — which is what makes the theorem useful in the (typical) case where it does not. ## Sources All material in this chapter is from Aditya Guntuboyina's Berkeley STAT 201A lecture notes (*FullLectureNotes201AFall2019*), as reconstructed section by section in `docs/statistics/berkeley/guntuboyina-notes/FullLectureNotes201AFall2019/` of the library repository.
